Capstone 8: AML transaction monitoring

← All capstones · Step-by-step build guide · Starter

Architecture and system design (read this first)

Before you write code, study how this system is designed. These five views are the target architecture for a production-grade build; reproduce and adapt them in your own repository, and keep them current as you build. Full explanations, Mermaid, draw.io, SVG and PNG sources and the architecture decision records are in architecture/.

1. Solution architecture

Solution architecture: transaction data arrives in batches from core systems (here the IBM AMLworld dataset); analysts work alerts and cases; the MLRO decides on suspicious transaction reports to the financial intelligence unit (the NFIU in Nigeria).

Sources: Mermaid · draw.io · SVG · PNG

2. Logical architecture

Logical architecture: loading moves raw files through a staging table into a clean transaction model; detection runs each scenario (a versioned SQL file with named parameters) over a window and emits deduplicated alerts with evidence; investigation groups alerts into cases with append-only decisions; effectiveness compares alerts with labels.

Sources: Mermaid · draw.io · SVG · PNG

3. Technical architecture

Technical architecture shows how the code is organised inside the Spring Boot 4 service: thin controllers that validate and translate errors, services that hold the business rules and transaction boundaries, and a persistence layer (JPA where entity behaviour and locking help, JdbcClient/SQL for reporting and bulk work). Cross-cutting concerns (configuration, health, metrics, scheduling, outbound HTTP) are framework features configured once. Package by feature in code; the layers here are logical.

Sources: Mermaid · draw.io · SVG · PNG

4. Infrastructure architecture

Infrastructure architecture shows where things run on the cheapest production-like target, a single VPS (for example SSDNodes). Only Caddy is reachable from the internet; it terminates TLS and forwards to aml-transaction-monitoring on Docker's internal network, so the database is never exposed (Docker port publishing bypasses ufw, so nothing else publishes ports). Images are built once by GitHub Actions, stored in GHCR by commit SHA, and pulled onto the server; backups leave the machine daily. Sizing and every command are in the deployment guide.

Sources: Mermaid · draw.io · SVG · PNG

5. Cloud architecture

Cloud architecture maps the service onto managed cloud building blocks, drawn for AWS (ECS Express Mode, the AWS-recommended path for new accounts since App Runner closed to new customers in 2026). The database sits in private subnets; credentials come from the secret store, never from the image; images are immutable and tagged by commit SHA. The same design on the other clouds:

Sources: Mermaid · draw.io · SVG · PNG

Key design decisions

  1. One deployable Spring Boot service (modular monolith) on PostgreSQL
  2. Detection logic as versioned SQL scenarios
  3. Deduplicated alerts by scenario, subject and window
  4. Append-only decisions enforced by the database
  5. Staging + transform loading with COPY

Weeks 7–12. Modules used: 1, 3, 4.

Business context

Anti-money-laundering (AML) laws require banks to monitor transactions for patterns that suggest laundering and to report suspicious activity to their financial intelligence unit (in Nigeria, the NFIU, through suspicious transaction reports). Unlike real-time fraud rules (Capstone 7), AML monitoring usually runs in batch over days or weeks of history, looking for typologies: structuring (many deposits just under a reporting threshold), fan-in / fan-out (many accounts paying into one, or one paying out to many), rapid movement (money in and straight out), and cycles (funds that return to where they started).

You'll build an AML monitoring service whose detection logic is mostly SQL: window functions, CTEs and well-chosen indexes over millions of transactions, with an alert-and-case workflow for analysts.

What you'll build

Detection scenarios (each a scheduled or on-demand job)

Scenario Logic (sketch)
Structuring ≥ N transactions from one account within 7 days, each between 80% and 100% of a configured threshold
Fan-in One account receives from ≥ N distinct counterparties within a window
Fan-out One account sends to ≥ N distinct counterparties within a window
Rapid movement ≥ X% of funds received are sent out within 24 hours
Simple cycle A → B → A (or A → B → C → A) within a window, via a recursive CTE with a depth limit
High-risk currency or payment format Configurable list (e.g. cash, cross-currency)

Each scenario is a SQL query in a versioned file (src/main/resources/scenarios/*.sql), parameterised with named parameters through JdbcClient, and produces alerts with the evidence (transaction IDs, totals, window).

Alert and case workflow

Method and path Purpose
POST /api/v1/scenario-runs Run one or all scenarios over a date range (async)
GET /api/v1/scenario-runs/{id} Status, duration, alerts generated per scenario
GET /api/v1/alerts?scenario=&status=&page= Alert queue
GET /api/v1/alerts/{id} Evidence: involved transactions and accounts
POST /api/v1/cases Group alerts into a case for investigation
POST /api/v1/cases/{id}/decisions NO_FURTHER_ACTION / FILE_SAR with mandatory narrative; immutable and audited
GET /api/v1/reports/scenario-effectiveness Using the dataset's labels: alerts, laundering transactions caught, precision per scenario

Rules and quality bar

  1. Deduplication: re-running a scenario over the same period must not create duplicate alerts (unique key on scenario + subject + window).
  2. Every scenario query has a documented EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before and after indexing, and runs in seconds on the HI-Small dataset.
  3. Thresholds and windows are configuration, versioned, and stored on each alert.
  4. Analysts' decisions are append-only.

Data

Dataset IBM Transactions for Anti Money Laundering (AMLworld): synthetic, labelled financial transactions generated from a multi-agent world model, with laundering typologies
Download https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/ealtman2019/ibm-transactions-for-anti-money-laundering-aml (free Kaggle account). Use HI-Small_Trans.csv (~5 million transactions) for Phase 1; the patterns file lists labelled laundering attempts by typology
Licence Community Data License Agreement – Sharing 1.0 (CDLA-Sharing-1.0): use, modify and share including commercially; shared data must stay under the same agreement
Attribution "IBM Transactions for Anti Money Laundering (AML), E. Altman et al., Kaggle, CDLA-Sharing-1.0." Background paper: Altman et al., Realistic Synthetic Financial Transactions for Anti-Money Laundering Models, NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks
Loading Load with COPY (fastest) or JDBC batches into a staging table, then transform into account/txn tables with SQL. Keep the load idempotent

Skills you'll demonstrate

Advanced SQL (joins, CTEs including recursive, window functions) (3.1), indexing and query plans (3.3), migrations for large tables (3.4), bulk loading with JDBC/COPY (3.5), immutable audit design (1.7), async jobs and Problem Details (4.2), configuration properties (4.4).

Acceptance criteria

Infrastructure and deployment

During loading, PostgreSQL needs 2 vCPU / 4 GB RAM / 20 GB storage (HI-Small is ~5M rows; tables plus indexes take a few GB). Increase maintenance_work_mem while creating indexes. The app itself is small (0.5 vCPU / 1 GB). Run scenario jobs on the VPS or locally; on cloud platforms use a managed PostgreSQL sized as above and remember to scale it down afterwards. CI from the starter (use a small fixture, never the full dataset, in CI); deploy with the deployment guide.

Stretch goals

  • Customer risk rating that combines alert history and transaction profile.
  • Graph exploration endpoint: an account's counterparties to depth 2 (recursive CTE), returned as nodes and edges for a UI.
  • Compare a scenario's SQL in PostgreSQL and MySQL 8.4 and explain the plan differences.

Interview talking points

  • How you translated AML typologies into SQL, and how you tested them.
  • The slowest scenario query and exactly how you made it fast.
  • Why alerts and decisions are immutable, and how you enforced it.

Step-by-step build guide: AML transaction monitoring

Work through the steps in order. Each step ends with a Done when check: don't move on until it passes. Commit after every step with a clear message, so your history tells the story of the build.

Before you start

  • Finish the topics listed under "Skills you'll demonstrate" in the brief, or study them alongside.
  • Read the architecture section and the ADRs. You will update both at the end.
  • Install Java 21 (Temurin), Docker Desktop, Git and IntelliJ IDEA (topic 1.1).

Step 1: Create your repository from the starter

git clone https://github.com/sundayayandele/java-zero-hire.git
mkdir aml-transaction-monitoring && cp -R java-zero-hire/phases/01-foundations/capstones/08-aml-transaction-monitoring/starter/. aml-transaction-monitoring/
cd aml-transaction-monitoring
git init -b main && git add . && git commit -m "Start from the AML transaction monitoring starter"

Create an empty public repository called aml-transaction-monitoring on GitHub, then:

git remote add origin https://github.com/<your-username>/aml-transaction-monitoring.git
git push -u origin main

Done when: the Actions tab shows the CI workflow running on your first push.

Step 2: Run it locally

cp .env.example .env          # set DB_PASSWORD to anything local
docker compose up --build
curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/health
./mvnw verify                 # needs Docker running (Testcontainers)

Done when: health returns {"status":"UP"} and ./mvnw verify is green. The base package is ng.itlearning.aml.

Step 3: Get the data

Never commit raw datasets; download them with a script. Add data/ to .gitignore first.

mkdir -p data
# IBM AMLworld (CDLA-Sharing-1.0): download HI-Small_Trans.csv and HI-Small_Patterns.txt from
# https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/ealtman2019/ibm-transactions-for-anti-money-laundering-aml (Kaggle account needed)

Copy the licence and attribution lines from the brief's Data section into your README now.

Done when: the files are in data/ and git status doesn't show them.

Step 4: Fast staging load

  1. Stage HI-Small_Trans.csv with COPY ... FROM STDIN (FORMAT csv, HEADER) through CopyManager.
  2. Transform with SQL into account and txn (timestamp, from, to, amount, currency, format, is_laundering).
  3. Keep it idempotent: truncate staging, upsert into the final tables.

Done when: About 5 million rows load in minutes; record the timing.

Step 5: Indexes for the scenarios

  1. Indexes on txn(from_account, ts) and txn(to_account, ts); consider BRIN on ts.
  2. Capture EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before and after for every scenario.

Done when: Every scenario query runs in seconds.

Step 6: Write the scenarios in SQL

  1. One file per scenario under src/main/resources/scenarios/: structuring, fan-in, fan-out, rapid movement, cycles (recursive CTE with a depth limit), high-risk format.
  2. Named parameters through JdbcClient; thresholds and windows from configuration.
  3. Each produces alerts with evidence (transaction IDs, totals, window).

Done when: Integration tests on a small hand-made dataset trigger each scenario exactly once.

Step 7: Scenario runs without duplicates

  1. POST /api/v1/scenario-runs (async) over a date range; record status and counts.
  2. Unique key on (scenario, subject, window) so re-runs create no duplicate alerts.

Done when: Running the same range twice leaves the alert count unchanged.

Step 8: Alerts, cases and decisions

  1. Alert queue with filters; alert detail with evidence.
  2. Cases group alerts; decisions NO_FURTHER_ACTION / FILE_SAR with a mandatory narrative, append-only and audited.

Done when: Tests prove decisions can't be edited or deleted.

Step 9: Scenario effectiveness

  1. Use is_laundering labels: alerts, laundering transactions caught and precision per scenario.
  2. Write up which scenario you'd tune first and why.

Done when: The effectiveness report is in your README.

Step 10: Deploy and automate

  1. Make sure ./mvnw verify and the GitHub Actions workflow are green on main.
  2. Optional: mirror the repository to gitlab.com so .gitlab-ci.yml runs too. Other platforms (Azure DevOps, AWS CodeBuild, Jenkins, Argo CD) are covered in the CI/CD guide.
  3. Deploy using the deployment guide: a single VPS (2 vCPU / 4 GB) is cheapest; AWS, Azure and GCP steps are there too.
  4. Put the public health URL (/actuator/health) at the top of your README.

Done when: the health URL returns UP from the internet, and no secret is in Git (git log -p | grep -i password finds nothing real).

Step 11: Update the architecture pack

  1. Copy the architecture/ folder from this capstone into your repository.
  2. Edit the Mermaid (.mmd) or draw.io (.drawio) files so all five diagrams match what you actually built; re-export SVG/PNG (draw.io: File → Export; Mermaid: npx @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli -i x.mmd -o x.svg).
  3. Write at least three ADRs of your own (copy the format in architecture/adr/): one for persistence, one for concurrency or performance, one you chose yourself.

Done when: someone can understand your system from the diagrams and ADRs without reading code.

Step 12: Write the README and record a demo

Your README must cover, in this order: the business problem; the architecture diagram; how to run it; API examples with curl; data sources and licences; design decisions and trade-offs; performance numbers (query plans, timings); what you'd do next. Then record a 3-minute demo video.

Done when: a hiring manager can read the README in three minutes and know what you built and why.

Step 13: Check against the rubric and submit

When you're stuck, go back to the topic in the brief's skills table, or ask in the course forum. For Capstones 1 and 2, your mentor shares the reference solution once your submission has passed, so you can compare approaches.
